findings.claim: Residual of R3-BYPASS-002 (over-blocking half): default SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL=jrnb2024 is a bare local-part that does not match the operator's local-git email james@brokai.net (local-part: james). Gate artefacts committed locally from that identity will be rejected by verify_gate_commit_author, making commit-author verification non-functional for the expected local-git workflow. The security concern (substring bypass via *${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}*) is fully closed by the v0.4 rewrite; only the operationally-blocking default remains. Documented workaround exists (SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS env var), but it must be set on every orchestrator invocation and is not the default.
findings.evidence: scripts/wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh line 51: SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL:-jrnb2024}". Line 115: local allowlist="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS:-${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}}". Lines 126-129: bare local-part branch: actual_local="${email%@*}"; candidate=jrnb2024; if [[ "$candidate" == "$actual_local" ]]. For email=james@brokai.net: actual_local=james; candidate=jrnb2024; 'jrnb2024 == james' → false → loop exhausted → return 1 → gate BLOCKS. For email=jrnb2024@users.noreply.github.com (GitHub web-UI default): actual_local=jrnb2024; match succeeds → pass. System context confirms operator email is james@brokai.net; git user is jrnb2024 (GitHub username, not email). Script comment (line 105) documents override: SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS="james@brokai.net:jrnb2024:james@anthropic.com". R3-BYPASS-002 mitigation explicitly requested "Change the default to james@brokai.net" — this was not implemented.
findings.impact: When the operator commits gate artefacts locally using their configured git identity james@brokai.net, every --gate invocation fails with 'committed by james@brokai.net (expected member of allowlist jrnb2024)'. The operator must either always commit via GitHub web-UI (where noreply address has local-part jrnb2024) or remember to export SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS on every orchestrator session. Persistent gate failure creates operational pressure to skip or permanently bypass the commit-author check, undermining the R-022-12 defence-in-depth invariant. Severity is MIN (not MAJ) because: the substring bypass attack surface is gone; GitHub web-UI commits work with the default; and the override procedure is documented inline.
findings.mitigation: Expand the default to cover both identities: SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL:-james@brokai.net}" (full email for local-git) and add SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY:-jrnb2024@users.noreply.github.com}" for GitHub web-UI commits. Seed the allowlist with both: local allowlist="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS:-${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}:${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY}}". Alternatively, change the default bare-local-part from jrnb2024 to james to match the local-git identity, and retain jrnb2024 as a second entry. Update §4.7 to document both accepted identities and their sources.

findings.claim: reviewer_id is a reviewer-controlled free-text field in SonnetReviewResult that sanitize_review_result does not sanitize. An adversarial reviewer can embed control characters, Unicode line-separators (U+2028/U+2029), or backtick sequences in reviewer_id. If the Opus orchestrator includes reviewer_id in fix-round Codex prompts (e.g., as provenance metadata for which reviewer raised which finding), the field carries unsanitized injection content into the Codex session.
findings.evidence: scripts/sanitize_review_finding.py sanitize_review_result() (lines 63-84): sanitizes summary, self_reported_concerns items, and findings[]. It does NOT sanitize reviewer_id, lens, or plan_version. SANITIZE_FIELDS tuple (line 41): ('id', 'claim', 'evidence', 'impact', 'mitigation') — reviewer_id is distinct from finding id and is not included. docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/r3-safety/dispatcher-result.json structured_review.reviewer_id: "r3-safety-bypass" — confirmed as a top-level result field whose value is emitted by the reviewer (Claude), not injected by the dispatch infrastructure. §4.3 invariant 9 enumerates sanitized fields as 'claim, evidence, impact, mitigation' — reviewer_id is omitted from the invariant.
findings.impact: Adversarial reviewer can inject prompt-injection payloads via reviewer_id that bypass all sanitization controls (control-char strip, Unicode-separator removal, backtick escape, length cap). Exploitability depends on whether the Opus orchestrator includes reviewer_id in Codex fix-round prompts. Given that reviewer_id is natural provenance metadata, inclusion is plausible. The field is not length-capped, so a large reviewer_id could also be used for context-window exhaustion.
findings.mitigation: Add reviewer_id to the set of top-level fields sanitized in sanitize_review_result(): apply sanitize_text(out['reviewer_id']) when present. Also sanitize lens and plan_version for defence-in-depth (both are nominally closed-enum/version strings but the schema does not enforce this at the sanitizer layer). Update §4.3 invariant 9 to enumerate all sanitized top-level fields, not just finding fields.

findings.claim: The _looks_like_review_result heuristic creates a shape-confusion attack surface: a finding dict that carries extra 'verdict' and 'findings' keys is routed through sanitize_review_result instead of sanitize_finding, causing the outer finding's own claim/evidence/impact/mitigation fields to go unsanitized. sanitize_review_result processes the nested 'findings' list but never calls sanitize_finding on the wrapping object itself.
findings.evidence: scripts/sanitize_review_finding.py lines 87-89: _looks_like_review_result returns True if 'verdict' in d and ('findings' in d or 'self_reported_concerns' in d). Lines 106-108: if _looks_like_review_result(parsed): cleaned = sanitize_review_result(parsed). sanitize_review_result (lines 63-84) processes out['summary'], out['self_reported_concerns'], and out['findings'], but not the top-level dict's own claim/evidence/impact/mitigation keys. An adversarial finding dict with extra keys {'id': '...', 'severity': 'CRIT', 'claim': '<INJECT>', 'evidence': '<INJECT>', 'verdict': 'APPROVED', 'findings': []} passes _looks_like_review_result=True, routes to sanitize_review_result, and exits with claim and evidence unsanitized. In the normal flow (full SonnetReviewResult piped as input), sanitize_review_result correctly reaches each finding via sanitize_finding — the attack requires the orchestrator to pipe an individual finding dict that masquerades as a result.
findings.impact: If the orchestrator ever pipes a single extracted finding dict to the sanitizer (rather than the full result or a flat array), an adversarial reviewer who added extra 'verdict'/'findings' keys to their finding objects can bypass sanitization of that finding's free-text fields. The impact is bounded by how the Opus orchestrator assembles fix-round prompts from individual findings; the full-result pipeline is unaffected.
findings.mitigation: Add a guard in sanitize_review_result to also sanitize any finding-shaped keys present at the top level: after processing summary/self_reported_concerns/findings, call sanitize_finding on the result dict itself. Alternatively, simplify _looks_like_review_result to require BOTH verdict and findings keys AND the absence of finding-specific keys (id, severity, claim) to exclude adversarially-shaped finding dicts. Document in §4.3 that the orchestrator MUST pipe the full SonnetReviewResult or a flat array to the sanitizer, never individual extracted finding dicts.

findings.claim: require_cmd python3 sha256sum in check_hash_chain is overly broad: python3 is not used anywhere inside check_hash_chain (only in resolve_real_path which is called from check_no_symlink_escape). On macOS where sha256sum is absent, require_cmd returns 6, the || branch checks for shasum (present), returns 0, and execution continues with python3 potentially missing — yet hash_file works correctly using shasum. The check nominally fails on a missing tool that is not actually required, creating confusing control flow and masking a genuine missing-prerequisite scenario if both sha256sum and shasum are absent but python3 is present.
findings.evidence: scripts/wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh lines 303-309: require_cmd python3 sha256sum || { if ! command -v shasum ...; return 6; fi }. hash_file() (lines 349-355) uses sha256sum or shasum only — no python3 call. resolve_real_path() (lines 81-93) uses python3 but is only called inside check_no_symlink_escape (line 207). On macOS: require_cmd python3 sha256sum returns 6 (sha256sum absent); || branch: shasum present → returns 0; execution continues; hash_file uses shasum correctly. If python3 is absent but shasum is present, same outcome — execution continues and hash_chain verification works without python3.
findings.impact: No security impact. The overly-broad prerequisite check means a missing python3 does not halt check_hash_chain on macOS, but python3 is not needed there. Diagnostic confusion if debugging prerequisite failures. Future maintainers may incorrectly conclude python3 is required in the hash-chain path and introduce an actual python3 dependency.
findings.mitigation: Remove python3 from the require_cmd call inside check_hash_chain: require_cmd sha256sum || { ... shasum fallback ... }. Add a separate require_cmd python3 guard at the start of check_no_symlink_escape where it is actually used. This makes prerequisite checks match actual usage.

self_reported_concerns: The unprotected pin-manifest window (plan-merge to 020K landing) is real but the threat model is sound: tampering the manifest without also compromising the ACC repo causes drift-detection pauses, not silent bypasses; a two-point attack requiring SCP-main and ACC-repo write access is an insider threat not addressable by CODEOWNERS alone. The window is accepted per §6 and I concur this is correctly scoped.

The _looks_like_review_result heuristic (R4-BYPASS-003) only matters if the orchestrator uses the individual-finding pipeline; the full-result pipeline is safe. I flag it MIN because the ACC orchestrator prompt-assembly logic is not auditable from this repo and the scenario is plausible.
structured_review.summary: v0.4 closes all three R3 MAJ/MIN safety findings and the nit carry-forward. R3-BYPASS-001 (hash-chain wrong paths): both branches now correctly use review-{lens}.json relative to terminal_dir — CLOSED. R3-BYPASS-002 (verify_gate_commit_author over/under-broad): the substring bypass attack (*${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}*) is eliminated; the new colon-separated allowlist with exact/local-part matching is semantically sound; the residual over-blocking of local-git commits from james@brokai.net is acknowledged with documented SCP_OPERATOR_EMAILS workaround — CLOSED with accepted residual (security concern resolved; operational gap is MIN, carried as R4-BYPASS-001). R3-BYPASS-003 (self_reported_concerns unsanitized): sanitize_review_result now sanitizes both summary and self_reported_concerns items — CLOSED. R3-BYPASS-004 (020J rollback missing numeric ID): §8 R-022-13 now explicitly requires capturing the id from the POST response, using it in the DELETE path, and verifying an empty tag-protection list before reporting status=blocked — CLOSED. R3-BYPASS-005 (CODEOWNERS forward-reference): §6 correctly documents the open window and the threat model acceptance — CLOSED as accepted residual. Fresh lens on v0.4 surfaces four findings, all MIN or nit: reviewer_id is a reviewer-controlled free-text field not reached by sanitize_review_result (R4-BYPASS-002 MIN); _looks_like_review_result shape-confusion can bypass sanitize_finding routing for adversarially-crafted finding dicts (R4-BYPASS-003 MIN); default jrnb2024 bare-local-part doesn't match james@brokai.net local-git commits, residual over-blocking from R3-BYPASS-002 (R4-BYPASS-001 MIN); require_cmd python3 sha256sum overly broad in check_hash_chain (R4-BYPASS-004 nit). No CRIT or MAJ findings remain. Verdict: APPROVED_WITH_FINDINGS.
